name: Christian Ethics

objectives.text: Identify the Ten Commandments as the rules God gave his people for how to live
Identify everyday actions such as lying and stealing as breaking God's commandments
Explain what it means to honor parents and others in authority according to the fifth commandment
Retell the parable of the Good Samaritan and explain whom Jesus calls our neighbor
Explain that God sees and knows everything we do, so right and wrong are measured by God and not by who is watching
Summarize the two greatest commandments and show how they sum up duties to God and duties to neighbor in the Ten Commandments
Explain why Christians tell the truth by connecting honesty to the truthful character of God
Apply the Golden Rule to school situations such as bullying, teasing, and leaving others out
Compare what the surrounding culture says is right with what the Bible teaches on a given moral question
Explain that each commandment both forbids a sin and requires the opposite duty, using the sixth commandment as an example
Explain how Scripture describes conscience and the moral law written on every human heart
Analyze Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount that God's law reaches the heart as well as outward actions
Explain the Reformed teaching that obedience to God's law is a response of gratitude for grace and not a way to earn salvation
Apply the doctrine of the image of God to the value of human life in issues such as abortion and euthanasia
Explain the biblical view of work as a calling from God and the Scripture's warnings against laziness
Explain the biblical teaching on marriage and sexual purity as grounded in creation and the seventh commandment
Explain what Scripture teaches about justice and mercy toward the poor and vulnerable
Compare consequence-based, duty-based, and virtue-based ethical theories with biblical ethics' attention to God's law, right motive, and God's glory
Explain the Reformed doctrine of Christian liberty and the care owed to a weaker brother in matters Scripture does not command
Construct a biblical framework for moral decision making that weighs direct commands, scriptural principles, wisdom, and conscience
Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and civil laws of the Old Testament and explain how the Reformed tradition applies each today
Evaluate complex ethical dilemmas such as war and bioethics using scriptural principles and the Reformed confessional tradition
Defend the existence of objective morality grounded in God's character against the claims of moral relativism
Distinguish the three uses of the law and explain the Reformed teaching on the law as a guide for the believer's life

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (Ten Commandments, two great commandments, truth-telling, Golden Rule, worldview comparison, Sermon on the Mount, law and grace, image of God, work, decision making, dilemmas, relativism, third use of the law). Dropped vague recall items or merged them into fuller objectives. Recast 'observe that God sees everything' as an explanation of God as the measure of right and wrong. Moved the Golden Rule earlier. Added missing competencies: honoring authority, the Good Samaritan, the forbids-and-requires reading of each commandment, conscience and natural law, marriage and sexual ethics, justice and mercy, comparison with secular ethical theories, Christian liberty, and the moral, ceremonial, and civil distinction. Added verse-level Scripture and confession anchors, removed whole-concept citations that did not fit, and left neighbouring material on holiness, prayer, and the fruit of the Spirit to the sibling sub-topics.
